title: Nuclear Weapons
scope: Nuclear arsenals: deterrence against abolition, and the climate and famine effects of nuclear war. Not reactors.

overview.summary: Whether nuclear arsenals prevent great-power war or risk catastrophe, and whether to strengthen, cut, ban or spread them.
overview.scope_covered: The world’s nuclear arsenals and what to do with them: deterrence, arms control, the ban treaty, the spread of weapons to new states, and the climate and famine effects of nuclear war.
overview.scope_excluded: Nuclear power and reactors; cyber, drone and gray-zone warfare and the wider international order, except where a camp’s case about nuclear weapons rests on them.
overview.why_now: On February 5, 2026 the New START treaty expired with no replacement, leaving US and Russian strategic nuclear weapons without a treaty cap for the first time since 1972. Russia had offered to keep observing its limits for a year; the United States did not formally answer.

stats.label: Nuclear warheads in the world
stats.note: Nine countries held an estimated 12,187 nuclear warheads in January 2026, down by more than four fifths from a peak of about 70,000 in 1986.
stats.detail: The Federation of American Scientists, whose estimates the series uses, puts the 1986 peak at “approximately 70,300.” Most of the fall came in the decade after the Cold War, through US–Soviet and US–Russian treaties and unilateral cuts. The total includes warheads retired and awaiting dismantlement as well as usable ones. In its 2026 estimates FAS says reductions have “slowed significantly compared with the 1990s” and continue only because retired weapons are being taken apart, while “military stockpiles (useable nuclear weapons) are increasing again.” SIPRI’s 2026 Yearbook puts the January 2026 military stockpile about 130 warheads higher than a year earlier and warns that new warheads may soon outpace dismantlement, so the total could rise for the first time since the 1980s. Every count is an estimate from public information, and SIPRI notes that most nuclear-armed states are becoming less transparent.
stats.source_label: Our World in Data, from Federation of American Scientists estimates

stats.label: Share of usable warheads held by Russia and the United States
stats.note: Russia, with about 4,400 usable warheads, and the United States, with about 3,700, hold about 83 percent of the 9,745 warheads in the world’s military stockpiles.
stats.detail: Counting retired warheads awaiting dismantlement, Russia holds about 5,420 and the United States about 5,042, almost 86 percent of all warheads. SIPRI describes both shares as slightly lower than in recent years, a trend it expects to continue as other arsenals grow. Both countries are replacing nearly every part of their nuclear forces: warheads, missiles, submarines, bombers and the factories that make them. SIPRI also estimates that Russia keeps about 1,794 shorter-range, non-strategic warheads in central storage, a class no treaty had limited as of 2026. The concentration cuts both ways in the debate. Those who favor negotiated cuts note that one bilateral deal could still cover most of the world’s weapons; those who favor stronger deterrence say bilateral limits no longer fit a world in which China is building up and Russia’s shorter-range arsenal sits outside every agreement.
stats.source_label: SIPRI Yearbook 2026, World nuclear forces (Kristensen and Korda)

stats.label: Warheads deployed on missiles and aircraft
stats.note: About 4,012 warheads were deployed on missiles and aircraft in January 2026; SIPRI estimates that 2,100 to 2,200 of them sat on ballistic missiles on high operational alert.
stats.detail: Warheads on high alert can be launched within minutes. SIPRI says nearly all of them belong to Russia and the United States, with smaller numbers kept by France and the United Kingdom, and that China and India may have begun placing some warheads on alert as well; its 2026 count includes about 34 deployed Chinese and 12 deployed Indian warheads, both new. The deployed total rose by about 100 from January 2025, mainly because SIPRI reassessed Russian deployments and added the Chinese and Indian ones. The rest of the stockpile sits in central storage and would need preparation before use. Launch time is at the center of the argument over de-alerting: arms-control advocates want to lengthen leaders’ decision time, while defenders of current postures say alert forces deter a disarming first strike.
stats.source_label: SIPRI Yearbook 2026, World nuclear forces (Kristensen and Korda)

stats.label: People without food two years after a nuclear war, by size of war
stats.note: A 2022 model found an India–Pakistan nuclear war could leave 255 million to 2.5 billion people without food after two years, a US–Russia war over 5 billion; its smoke estimates are disputed.
stats.detail: The authors model a one-week war in which burning cities loft soot, measured in teragrams (Tg, millions of tonnes), into the stratosphere, where it dims sunlight and cools the planet for years. The figures count people who would starve by the end of year two if everyone else received a minimum diet of 1,911 kilocalories a day, with no international trade and half of livestock feed diverted to people. They come on top of deaths from the blasts themselves, which the same table puts at 27 million in the smallest scenario and 360 million in the largest. The population base is the 6.7 billion people of 2010, and the authors call the scenarios “illustrative examples.” The contested step is the first one: how much soot would reach the stratosphere at all.
stats.source_label: Xia, Robock et al., Nature Food (2022), Table 1

stats.label: New START limit on each side’s deployed strategic warheads
stats.note: From 2011 until it lapsed in February 2026, New START held the United States and Russia to 1,550 deployed strategic warheads and 700 deployed missiles and bombers each.
stats.detail: The treaty also capped each side at 800 deployed and non-deployed launchers and provided for on-site inspections and data exchanges, which Russia suspended in 2023. On February 11, 2026 Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Russia would stay within the old limits “only as long as the United States does not exceed the above limits.” The Federation of American Scientists estimates that by loading stored warheads onto existing missiles, the United States could roughly double its ICBM warheads from 400 to about 800 and add 400 to 500 on submarines, while Russia could add about 400 on ICBMs and 200 to 300 on submarines. The Union of Concerned Scientists says deployed forces on both sides “could double” within a few years without limits. Arms Control Today’s September 2026 issue reported that at an August Defense Department briefing, officials had not said whether the United States would add deployed strategic forces.
stats.source_label: Arms Control Today, New START Expires As U.S. Urges ‘Modernized’ Treaty (March 2026)

stats.label: Deaths in Hiroshima within months of the 1945 atomic bombing
stats.note: The Hiroshima bomb killed an estimated 90,000 to 166,000 of the city’s roughly 340,000 to 350,000 people within two to four months, and the Nagasaki bomb 60,000 to 80,000.
stats.detail: Nagasaki had an estimated 250,000 to 270,000 people at the time. The Radiation Effects Research Foundation, a joint Japanese–US research body, says exact figures will never be known: military records were destroyed, whole families died with no one left to report them, and the number of forced laborers in both cities is unknown. These remain the only uses of nuclear weapons in war. Those who seek abolition cite the bombings as proof of what the weapons do to a city; those who favor deterrence cite the horror they revealed as a reason the weapons have not been used since.
stats.source_label: Radiation Effects Research Foundation, Frequently Asked Questions

stats.label: Documented cases of near nuclear use, 1962–2002
stats.note: A 2014 Chatham House study listed 13 incidents from 1962 to 2002 when nuclear weapons nearly were used through error, miscalculation or crisis; deterrence advocates read them as safeguards holding.
stats.detail: The cases include four during the Cuban missile crisis of 1962; the 1973 Arab–Israeli war; false warnings at the North American Aerospace Defense Command in 1979 and 1980, from a training tape and a faulty computer chip; the 1983 Soviet false alarm, when duty officer Stanislav Petrov judged a reported US launch to be an error; the NATO exercise Able Archer in 1983; the failed Soviet coup of 1991; the 1995 Norwegian research rocket that Russia briefly took for a missile; and the India–Pakistan crises of 1999 and 2001–2002. The authors conclude that the world “has, indeed, been lucky” and that individual judgment, “often in disobedience of protocol,” prevented catastrophe several times.
stats.source_label: Chatham House, Too Close for Comfort (Lewis, Williams, Pelopidas and Aghlani, 2014)

stats.label: Usable warheads held by the seven smaller nuclear powers
stats.note: In January 2026 the largest arsenal outside Russia and the United States was China’s, about 620 warheads and growing faster than any other; the smallest was North Korea’s, about 60.
stats.detail: The figures are SIPRI’s January 2026 estimates of military stockpiles; France also holds about 80 retired warheads. Federation of American Scientists estimates put China at about 350 warheads in 2020. The US Defense Department’s December 2025 report to Congress, as quoted by FAS, said China’s stockpile “remained in the low 600s through 2024, reflecting a slower rate of production,” but that China “remains on track to have over 1,000 warheads by 2030,” and has likely loaded more than 100 missile silos in three new silo fields. Even at 1,000, China would hold several thousand fewer warheads than Russia or the United States. As of 2026, China had declined to join trilateral arms-control talks and kept a declared policy of no first use. North Korea’s figure counts assembled warheads; SIPRI says it has fissile material for at least 90. Israel has never confirmed that it has nuclear weapons.
stats.source_label: SIPRI Yearbook 2026, World nuclear forces (Kristensen and Korda)

stats.label: Spending on nuclear weapons by the nine nuclear-armed states
stats.note: The campaign group ICAN estimates that the nine nuclear-armed states spent $118.8 billion on nuclear weapons in 2025, up 19 percent from 2024, with the United States spending $69.2 billion.
stats.detail: ICAN, which campaigns for abolition, builds the figures from budget documents where they exist and estimates them where they do not. For Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Israel and North Korea it calculates shares of total military spending, so those numbers are rougher than the US, British and French ones. Its country estimates are China $13.5 billion, the United Kingdom $12.6 billion, Russia $9.5 billion, France $7.7 billion, India $2.8 billion, Pakistan $1.5 billion, Israel $1.2 billion and North Korea $0.66 billion. ICAN puts the five-year total for 2021–2025 at $471 billion and says at least 25 companies earned about $38 billion from nuclear-weapons work in 2025.
stats.source_label: ICAN, Premeditated: 2025 Global Nuclear Weapons Spending (June 2026)

stats.label: Countries in the main nuclear treaties
stats.note: As of September 2026, the 2017 Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons had 75 parties and 96 signatories, none nuclear-armed; the UN counted 191 members of the 1968 Non-Proliferation Treaty.
stats.detail: India, Pakistan and Israel never joined the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. Under Article VI the five recognized nuclear-weapon states, the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France and China, promise to pursue negotiations “in good faith” on nuclear disarmament. NPT review conferences failed to agree a final document in 2015, 2022 and 2026; the last agreed outcome was in 2010. UN News reported that the 2026 conference broke up in May, deadlocked over Iran. The ban treaty entered into force in January 2021; the most recent to join, as of September 2026, were Ghana and Kyrgyzstan in September 2025 and Tonga in July 2026. No NATO member and no country under a US nuclear umbrella, such as Japan, South Korea or Australia, had joined. The treaty’s first review conference was scheduled for November 30 to December 4, 2026, at the UN in New York, according to ICAN.
stats.source_label: UN Treaty Collection, Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, status

stats.label: Nuclear test explosions since 1945
stats.note: Eight countries have carried out 2,056 nuclear test explosions since 1945, 1,030 of them by the United States and 715 by the Soviet Union and Russia.
stats.detail: Of the 2,056, 528 were in the atmosphere and 1,528 underground. The other counts are France 210, China 45, the United Kingdom 45, North Korea 6, India 3 and Pakistan 2. As of 2025, the last tests were by the Soviet Union in October 1990, the United Kingdom in November 1991, the United States in September 1992, France in January 1996, China in July 1996, India and Pakistan in May 1998, and North Korea in September 2017. The 1996 Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty had not entered into force as of 2025. On October 29, 2025 President Trump said, as NBC News reported, that he had told the military “to start testing our Nuclear Weapons on an equal basis”; Energy Secretary Chris Wright later said the tests would not include nuclear explosions, according to Fortune. Arms-control and abolition groups oppose a return to explosive testing; some deterrence advocates, including the Heritage Foundation, want the United States ready to test.
stats.source_label: Arms Control Association, The Nuclear Testing Tally

stats.label: Forecast chance that nuclear weapons kill over 10 million people by 2045
stats.note: Asked in 2024 for the chance that nuclear weapons kill more than 10 million people by 2045, 110 experts gave a median of 5 percent, 41 superforecasters 1 percent and a public sample 10 percent.
stats.detail: Superforecasters are people with strong track records in forecasting tournaments. The same experts judged that six relatively achievable policies, led by a crisis communications network among nuclear powers and “failsafe” reviews of nuclear command systems, would together roughly halve the risk, but gave those two policies only about a 15 percent chance of being adopted within three years. In a 2022 tournament run by the same institute, superforecasters put the chance of a nuclear catastrophe killing at least 10 percent of humanity by 2100 at 4 percent and domain experts at 8 percent. These are judgments, not measurements. Those who favor deterrence cite such numbers as evidence that the risk is small; those who favor abolition, as evidence that it adds up over decades.
stats.source_label: Forecasting Research Institute, Can Humanity Achieve a Century of Nuclear Peace? (2024)

stats.label: Projected cost of US nuclear forces, 2025–2034
stats.note: The Congressional Budget Office projected in 2025 that US plans to operate, sustain and modernize nuclear forces would cost $946 billion over 2025–2034, about $95 billion a year.
stats.detail: The total includes $357 billion to operate and sustain the forces, $309 billion to modernize delivery systems and weapons, $72 billion for the weapons laboratories and production complex, $79 billion for command, control, communications and early warning, and $129 billion for likely cost overruns, estimated from historical cost growth. It is 25 percent ($190 billion) more than CBO’s 2023 projection of $756 billion for 2023–2032. The largest single program is the Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile, whose estimated cost rose 81 percent to about $141 billion in 2024 after a Pentagon review, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
stats.source_label: Congressional Budget Office, Projected Costs of U.S. Nuclear Forces, 2025 to 2034

stats.label: Doomsday Clock setting
stats.note: In January 2026 the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists set its Doomsday Clock at 85 seconds to midnight, then its closest ever; deterrence advocates do not treat the setting as a measure of risk.
stats.detail: The clock is a symbol set each year by the Bulletin’s Science and Security Board, which weighs nuclear risk alongside climate change, biological threats and disruptive technologies. Its farthest setting was 17 minutes to midnight in 1991, after the Cold War ended and the first Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty was signed. In its January 27, 2026 statement the board cited the coming expiry of New START, open talk of using nuclear weapons for coercion, spending on arsenal expansion, and more non-nuclear countries considering the bomb. The Bulletin advocates arms control and disarmament.
stats.source_label: Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, Doomsday Clock timeline

stats.label: South Koreans who support their country having nuclear weapons
stats.note: In the Asan Institute’s 2026 annual poll, a record 80 percent of South Koreans supported their country acquiring its own nuclear weapons, up from 76.2 percent in 2025.
stats.detail: The same poll found 60.4 percent support for bringing US tactical nuclear weapons back to South Korea. Support falls when respondents are told of costs such as sanctions or hosting facilities nearby, which Asan has examined in a separate brief. South Korea belongs to the Non-Proliferation Treaty, and as of 2026 its government under President Lee Jae-myung had not sought nuclear weapons. The poll matters to the debate because the case for national bombs, a minority view among experts, has majority public backing in at least one close US ally.
stats.source_label: Asan Institute for Policy Studies, South Koreans and Their Neighbors 2026

stats.label: Living atomic-bomb survivors (hibakusha)
stats.note: At the end of March 2026, 91,105 people held Japan’s atomic-bomb survivor certificate, 8,025 fewer than a year earlier; their average age was 86.66.
stats.detail: The number is less than a quarter of its 1981 peak, the same report says, and 8,800 certified survivors died during the year; about 2,061 live outside Japan. The survivors’ organization Nihon Hidankyo won the 2024 Nobel Peace Prize, which the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded “for its efforts to achieve a world free of nuclear weapons and for demonstrating through witness testimony that nuclear weapons must never be used again.” As the last witnesses die, campaigners and museums are working to preserve their testimony.
stats.source_label: Chugoku Shimbun, Hiroshima Peace Media Center, reporting Japan’s health ministry

questions.text: Have nuclear weapons kept the peace between great powers since 1945?
questions.why: No great powers have fought each other directly since 1945, the longest such stretch in centuries. But history offers no control case, and trade, alliances, democracy and the memory of two world wars changed at the same time.
questions.detail:
Those who credit the bomb point to four decades in which the United States and the Soviet Union confronted each other over Berlin, Cuba and the Middle East without fighting directly, something rival great powers had rarely managed, and to leaders on both sides who recorded that the prospect of nuclear destruction shaped their choices. Nuclear-armed India and Pakistan have fought only limited clashes since 1998, and in May 2025, by SIPRI’s account, both took deliberate steps to keep their conflict conventional. Russia invaded non-nuclear Ukraine but, as of 2026, had not attacked NATO territory.

Skeptics answer that the record includes repeated near-uses, several averted by individuals who broke protocol, so the absence of nuclear war may owe as much to luck as to design. Wars involving nuclear states happened anyway: Korea, Vietnam, the 1969 Sino-Soviet border clashes, Kargil in 1999 and Russia’s war in Ukraine. And eight decades say little about a risk that compounds, since a small yearly chance of failure grows large over a century.

questions.text: Is a standing risk of nuclear catastrophe an acceptable price for the security deterrence provides?
questions.why: People who agree on the facts still weigh them differently. One side sets deterrence against the conventional world wars it may prevent; the other sets it against the irreversible loss of most of humanity, however unlikely.
questions.detail:
To those who accept the price, every security policy carries risk, and the alternative to deterrence is not a world without danger but one in which aggressive states with conventional or hidden nuclear advantages can coerce their neighbors. The two world wars killed tens of millions without nuclear weapons. Managing the risk through safety, communication and prudent doctrine, on this view, beats abandoning the tool that makes great-power war unthinkable.

To those who reject it, a policy that works only if it never fails once, under every future leader, will eventually fail, and its failure would not resemble a conventional war. The International Committee of the Red Cross holds that no adequate humanitarian response to nuclear use is possible. Accepting a few percent per generation of losing civilization, they argue, is a bet no government has the right to place on behalf of the rest of the world.

questions.text: Would a large nuclear war cause a nuclear winter and global famine?
questions.why: If enough soot reaches the stratosphere, sunlight drops and harvests fail for years. The dispute is over how much smoke burning cities would make and how high it would rise, which no experiment can test.
questions.detail:
Studies led by Alan Robock, Owen Brian Toon and Lili Xia, linking climate, crop and fishery models, find that even a regional war could leave hundreds of millions or more without food, and they point to large modern wildfires that have lofted smoke into the stratosphere just as the models assume. A 2018 Los Alamos study by Reisner and colleagues, which simulated the firestorms of a 100-weapon India–Pakistan exchange in detail, found that most soot stayed below about 12 km, where rain washes it out, and that “none of the simulations produced a nuclear winter effect.” Skeptics add that modern cities may burn less intensely than assumed and that war plans may not strike cities on the scale the scenarios use.

A 2025 consensus report from the US National Academies concluded that “too many uncertainties remained” to say how a nuclear war would affect the climate, while agreeing that if large amounts of soot did reach the upper atmosphere, substantial global cooling would follow.

questions.text: Would a bigger US arsenal deter Russia and China together, or set off an arms race?
questions.why: The United States is the only nuclear power planning against two nuclear rivals at once, and no one knows how many warheads that takes or how Moscow and Beijing would answer a US buildup.
questions.detail:
The congressional Strategic Posture Commission concluded in 2023 that the United States will soon face “two nuclear peer adversaries” and recommended preparing to increase deployed warheads and production capacity. If Russia and China coordinate, its supporters argue, forces sized for one rival may not deter both. The Heritage Foundation argues that loading stored warheads onto existing missiles is cheap and the surest way to bring rivals to the table, and notes that China’s buildup began while the United States was cutting.

The Arms Control Association and the Union of Concerned Scientists answer that a US buildup would invite Russia to upload its own reserves and China to speed up, leaving everyone spending more for less security. Deterrence, they argue, rests on the ability to retaliate, not on matching every warhead, so the United States can hold China at risk with far fewer weapons than it has, and mutual adherence to the old limits would keep both stability and leverage to bring China into talks.

questions.text: Does the treaty banning nuclear weapons bring disarmament closer?
questions.why: The ban treaty’s members are states without the bomb or a nuclear umbrella. Whether a norm they adopt can change the behavior of states that rely on the weapons is a prediction about politics, with partial precedents on both sides.
questions.detail:
Supporters argue that a legal prohibition works before it binds everyone: it raises the political price of nuclear threats and new deployments, moves banks, investors and companies away from weapons work, and gives the majority of states, who kept their side of the Non-Proliferation Treaty bargain, a way to show that the disarmament the nuclear states promised has stalled. Public opinion in several umbrella states favors joining.

Skeptics answer that no weapon will be dismantled under a treaty no nuclear-armed state has signed, that the ban has no verification system able to confirm an arsenal’s elimination, and that it divides the NPT community needed to stop proliferation. It presses mainly on open democracies, where public opinion matters, while Russia, China and North Korea ignore it, which could weaken deterrence among the states least likely to misuse it. Japan’s government says the treaty offers no practical path without the nuclear states.

questions.text: Would the world be safer if more threatened states had their own nuclear weapons?
questions.why: If nuclear weapons deter, giving them to threatened states should deter those states’ attackers too; if they are dangerous, every new owner adds new chances of accident, theft or war.
questions.detail:
The case for wider ownership rests on the record of states that gave up the bomb or never built it and were later attacked, set against those that built it and were left alone, and on the theory that nuclear-armed states treat one another with caution. Its supporters see allies such as South Korea and Poland, facing nuclear-armed neighbors, doubting how long US guarantees will last.

The case against holds that every new arsenal brings new command systems, new rival pairs and new chances for accident, unauthorized use or theft, and that some new owners would be unstable. Proliferation by US allies could unravel the Non-Proliferation Treaty and set off cascades: Japan after South Korea, Saudi Arabia after Iran, Turkey and others. New nuclear states are most exposed in the years before their forces can survive a first strike, which can tempt rivals to strike first, and under US law sanctions and a loss of US support would follow.

The US and Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites in 2025 and 2026 are read both ways: as proof that force can stop a program short of a bomb, and as proof that only a finished bomb keeps a state from being attacked.

questions.text: Is it morally permissible to threaten the mass killing of civilians to prevent war?
questions.why: Deterrence works by threatening retaliation that would kill vast numbers of people who did not choose their government’s aggression. Whether a threat meant never to be carried out differs morally from the act has divided ethicists and churches since the 1950s.
questions.detail:
Defenders of the threat argue that a threat never executed kills no one, and that if it prevents aggression and great-power war it saves lives. Modern targeting doctrine aims at military targets, and a state can hold a deterrent while working toward reductions; the Catholic bishops of the 1980s accepted deterrence on that condition. Giving it up unilaterally would hand coercive power to regimes with fewer scruples.

Critics argue that a credible threat requires a real readiness to kill millions, and that making that readiness permanent corrupts the states that hold it. Pope Francis said in 2019 that “the possessing of nuclear weapons is immoral,” and Pope Leo XIV has said nuclear deterrence “is based on the irrationality of relations between nations,” as Vatican News recounted in 2026. Even strikes aimed at military targets, they add, would kill civilians on a massive scale through fire, fallout and famine.

questions.text: Could a world without nuclear weapons be verified and kept stable?
questions.why: Even supporters of eventual abolition differ over whether it could work. Knowledge cannot be uninvented, and the closer the world gets to zero, the more a few hidden weapons would matter.
questions.detail:
Optimists note that verification has moved far beyond Cold War tools: on-site inspections under past treaties, the test-ban organization’s global seismic and radionuclide network, satellite imaging and new methods for confirming that warheads have been dismantled. South Africa built and then dismantled its weapons under international inspection. A cheater near zero, they add, would face a united coalition with large conventional forces and the ability to rebuild.

Skeptics answer that small stocks of fissile material are easy to hide, as the histories of Iraq, Iran and North Korea show. At zero, a handful of secret weapons would give decisive leverage, so every crisis would become a race to rebuild, and deterrence experts argue that some arsenal, however small, is more stable than none. The deadlock over Iran’s program at the 2026 NPT review conference shows how hard shared conclusions about compliance are even under the existing system.

positions.name: Strengthen nuclear deterrence
positions.steelman: Nuclear weapons are why the great powers have not fought a world war since 1945. Keep them modern, credible and sized for Russia and China together, or invite coercion.
positions.detail:
The danger today comes not from deterrence but from its erosion. Russia brandishes nuclear threats to shield its war in Ukraine, China is building up faster than anyone, North Korea is expanding, and Iran has sought the bomb. The United States must now deter two nuclear powers at once with forces designed in the 1980s and a production complex that has not built a fully new warhead in decades; the newest weapon in its arsenal is more than 35 years old, as the Heritage Foundation points out. A credible deterrent must be modern, survivable, sized against both rivals together and backed by a clear will to respond if attacked. Extended deterrence also stops proliferation: allies who trust the US umbrella do not need bombs of their own.

We support arms control that is verifiable and covers China and Russia’s shorter-range weapons, and disarmament is a worthy distant goal. But giving up weapons while adversaries keep theirs invites coercion, as Ukraine learned. The close calls of the Cold War led to hotlines, better safeguards and sturdier command systems; the answer to the risk of failure is a more robust deterrent, not a weaker one. Some of us would maintain and modernize today’s forces, as NATO does, saying that as long as nuclear weapons exist it will remain a nuclear alliance. Others would add warheads and missile defenses. France and the United Kingdom are extending their own deterrents to cover European allies.
positions.proponents: NATO; Heritage Foundation; Congressional Commission on the Strategic Posture of the United States; Emmanuel Macron

positions.name: Reduce arsenals step by step
positions.steelman: Deterrence cannot be wished away, but today’s arsenals are far bigger than it requires. Negotiated, verifiable limits brought warheads down before and can do it again.
positions.detail:
The more weapons there are, on higher alert and in more hands, the greater the chance that one is used by mistake. The way out is the one that has already worked. Treaties from SALT to New START cut the arsenals by tens of thousands, and the INF Treaty eliminated a whole class of missiles, 2,692 of them by June 1991 by the Arms Control Association’s count. Each agreement brought inspections, data exchanges and predictability, which curb the worst-case planning that drives arms races. With New START gone, the United States and Russia should keep to its limits while negotiating a successor, bring China into talks on reducing risk, keep the moratorium on explosive testing and lengthen leaders’ decision time. Our goal is a world without nuclear weapons, reached at the pace security allows and with the nuclear states at the table.

Some of us, such as Japan’s government and most NATO members, stress keeping deterrence strong while reductions proceed. Others, including the Arms Control Association, the Union of Concerned Scientists and the Back from the Brink campaign, also want no-first-use or sole-purpose policies, missiles taken off hair-trigger alert and an end to a single president’s sole authority to launch. To abolitionists who say step-by-step has stalled for decades, we answer that nothing is dismantled without the nuclear states, and that the reductions of the past forty years came from exactly this kind of diplomacy, which has paused before and can restart.
positions.proponents: Arms Control Association; Union of Concerned Scientists; Rose Gottemoeller; Government of Japan

positions.name: Ban nuclear weapons now
positions.steelman: Nuclear weapons are built to kill civilians by the city, and deterrence is a bet that no leader or warning system ever fails. They must be banned and stigmatized, like chemical weapons.
positions.detail:
Any use would violate the most basic principles of humanity and international humanitarian law. Today’s arsenals could end modern civilization, and a war between even the smaller nuclear powers could starve billions, with no government or aid agency able to respond. History records repeated near-misses averted by chance, and a risk run every year eventually comes due. The nuclear-armed states promised in Article VI of the Non-Proliferation Treaty, more than fifty years ago, to negotiate disarmament in good faith. Instead they are modernizing and growing their stockpiles and blocking even a mention of the ban treaty at the NPT. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons makes possession illegitimate, and its path to elimination is open to every nuclear state willing to join.

Norms change behavior before they bind everyone: the landmine and cluster-munition bans reduced use and production even by states that never signed, and the ban treaty already shapes investment decisions and public debate in countries under a nuclear umbrella. Step-by-step disarmament has had decades and delivered modernization instead. We work through law and the treaty, as ICAN and states parties such as Austria, Ireland, Mexico and South Africa do; through moral teaching, as the Holy See does; through humanitarian witness, as the International Committee of the Red Cross and the survivors of Nihon Hidankyo do; and through divestment campaigns and city resolutions.
positions.proponents: International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN); International Committee of the Red Cross; Holy See; Nihon Hidankyo; Austria; Ireland; Mexico; South Africa

positions.name: Let threatened states build their own bombs
positions.steelman: A bomb is the one sure guarantee against a nuclear-armed neighbor, and a distant ally’s promise lasts only until its next election. Stable, threatened states should be free to build their own.
positions.detail:
The record is stark. Ukraine gave up the Soviet nuclear weapons on its soil in 1994 in exchange for security assurances and was invaded twice by one of the guarantors. Libya gave up its program and its government was overthrown. Iran stayed short of a bomb and was bombed in 2025 and again in 2026. North Korea built one and has not been attacked. The logic the nuclear powers apply to themselves applies equally to threatened democracies such as South Korea, which faces a nuclear North Korea and a growing Chinese arsenal. Letting capable, stable allies defend themselves would also let the United States shed commitments and the risk of being drawn into their wars.

The nuclear age has produced no war between nuclear states larger than border clashes, and the stable democracies most likely to seek bombs today would manage them at least as responsibly as the existing nine. The cascade our critics fear is already under way, driven by weakening US guarantees and by Russian and North Korean threats. Some of us are realists in the tradition of Kenneth Waltz, who saw the spread of nuclear weapons as stabilizing in general, even to Iran. Others, like John Mearsheimer writing on Ukraine in 1993 or Doug Bandow at the Cato Institute on South Korea, back only selective proliferation by stable US allies. Most South Koreans who want a national bomb also want to keep the US alliance.
positions.proponents: John Mearsheimer; Doug Bandow; Cheong Seong-chang

positions.name: Prepare to survive a nuclear war
positions.steelman: Whichever side wins the deterrence debate, the weapons will exist for decades. Preparing to limit the damage, above all the famine after a war, is insurance against every other policy failing.
positions.detail:
Prevention matters most, and we do not ask anyone to give it up. But almost all the work and money in this field goes to the time before the first detonation and almost none to what comes after, when decisions would determine whether a single use becomes a global war and a war becomes a global famine. Founders Pledge estimated in 2023 that work on what happens after first use makes up at most about one in thirty grants in nuclear-security philanthropy. In the famine models, starvation kills many times more people than the blasts, and starvation is preventable: food can be grown in greenhouses, from seaweed and through industrial processes, if plans and supply chains are ready and trade continues. A 2024 study by ALLFED researchers found that in a severe nuclear-winter scenario, scaling up such “resilient foods” and keeping trade open could in principle feed the whole world, while without them the model predicts global famine.

The Red Cross is right that no adequate response is possible for the cities struck, but that is not true for the billions far from any blast whose survival would depend on food. The evidence that preparation makes war more thinkable is weak, and leaving billions to starve for want of planning is not a moral position. Some of us work on food and supply chains, as ALLFED does; some on managing escalation and keeping adversaries talking after a first use, the “right of boom” agenda Founders Pledge promotes; and some on civil defense, in the tradition of Switzerland, which has kept shelter space for its whole population for decades.
positions.proponents: Alliance to Feed the Earth in Disasters (ALLFED); Founders Pledge

crux.lead: Do nuclear weapons, kept indefinitely, prevent catastrophic war or only postpone it?
crux.subtitle: Every camp wants to avoid a nuclear war. They divide over whether the weapons are the main thing preventing one or the main thing that could cause one, and over how to weigh a small, lasting chance of catastrophe against the wars it may deter.
crux.empirical: How much of the long peace among great powers deterrence explains; how likely nuclear use is each year with more or fewer weapons, higher or lower alert and more or fewer owners; whether buildups or limits make rivals hold back; and how much smoke a war would send high into the sky, which decides whether any nuclear war becomes a global famine.
crux.values: How much a small chance of losing most of humanity should weigh against the security deterrence is meant to give people now; whether threatening to kill millions of civilians is permissible if the threat is never meant to be carried out; and whether states may stake the lives of people who have no say over their arsenals. Two people with the same facts can choose different camps.

actions.title: Read the Federation of American Scientists’ Status of World Nuclear Forces
actions.description: A regularly updated, sourced count of every country’s nuclear warheads, deployed and stored, with the history since 1945, by the analysts who also write SIPRI’s nuclear chapter.

actions.title: Read the National Academies report on the environmental effects of nuclear war
actions.description: The 2025 consensus report, commissioned by the US Congress, weighs the competing studies of nuclear winter and famine and sets out what is known and what is not. Free to read online.

actions.title: Tell your representative in Congress what US nuclear policy should be
actions.description: Contact your member of the House about nuclear spending, testing, arms control or the ban treaty, whatever your view; Congress funds and oversees every part of US nuclear policy.

actions.title: Read NATO’s case for nuclear deterrence
actions.description: NATO’s official explanation of why the alliance keeps nuclear weapons, how nuclear sharing works, and its stated commitment to creating the conditions for a world without them.

actions.title: Support the Arms Control Association
actions.description: A nonpartisan membership group that publishes Arms Control Today and presses for verifiable limits on nuclear arsenals, including restoring US–Russian limits after New START.

actions.title: Ask your city to join the ICAN Cities Appeal
actions.description: A campaign for city councils to call on their national governments to join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, with a template letter and steps for residents.

actions.title: Read John Mearsheimer’s case for a Ukrainian nuclear deterrent
actions.description: The 1993 Foreign Affairs essay arguing that Ukraine should keep the Soviet weapons on its soil to deter Russia, now widely cited by those who say threatened states need bombs. May require a subscription.
actions.for_position: Let threatened states build their own bombs

actions.title: Support ALLFED’s research on feeding everyone after a catastrophe
actions.description: The Alliance to Feed the Earth in Disasters researches and plans food supplies that could keep people fed after a nuclear winter or another sudden loss of sunlight.
actions.for_position: Prepare to survive a nuclear war

actions.title: Join a local hub of Back from the Brink
actions.description: A US coalition campaigning for no first use, an end to a president’s sole authority to launch, missiles off hair-trigger alert and a verifiable agreement to eliminate arsenals.

actions.title: See what a nuclear weapon would do to your city with NUKEMAP
actions.description: An interactive map by historian of science Alex Wellerstein that models the blast, heat and fallout of real and hypothetical weapons over any place you choose.

primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: one compact coastal scene grouped in the center with wide white margins, nothing touching the edges: a tall slim ballistic missile standing upright in an open round silo on the crest of a low rounded hill on the left, the dominant focal mass, filled; the round silo lid lying open beside the silo, filled with the same light tint as everything else; a medium ballistic missile submarine riding low in the sea at the right, its sail and long hull filled, its bow overlapping the foot of the hill; a small long-winged bomber aircraft flying just above and right of the missile nose, filled; one single continuous ground line crosses the whole scene, rising over the hill and running down into a gently wavy sea surface under the submarine, as the connective element; the hill is filled only down to a soft gentle curve just below the ground line, never a flat bottom edge.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #b3404f, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: mushroom clouds, explosions, fire, smoke, radiation trefoil symbols, skulls, doves, peace signs, broken or crossed-out missiles, flags, national markings, warning signs, countdown clocks, red buttons, globes with targets, crosshairs, people, faces.
